opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few reasons, and they reinforce each other.

The first is control. When an enterprise builds on an open model, they can run it wherever they want: on their own cloud account, on-prem, close to their data. For many companies, especially in regulated industries like finance or healthcare, the data simply can't leave certain boundaries. Open models let you bring the model to the data rather than the other way around.

The second is customization. Enterprises have very specific data and very specific tasks. With an open model you can fine-tune it, distill it, and adapt it to your domain. Often a smaller fine-tuned model does as well as, or better than, a much bigger general-purpose model on a narrow task, at a fraction of the cost and latency. That matters a lot when you go from a prototype to millions of requests a day.

The third is cost and predictability. With a proprietary API you're paying per token, and the provider can change the pricing, the model, or its behavior under you. With an open model you control the version, so the behavior doesn't silently shift, and you can optimize the serving stack and hardware yourself.

And finally there's the quality trajectory. A couple of years ago the gap between the best proprietary models and open models was quite large. That gap has narrowed a lot, and for many enterprise use cases the open models are now good enough. Once something is good enough, control, customization, and cost start to dominate the decision.

I'd also add that enterprises are typically not going to use just one model. They'll use a mix: maybe a frontier proprietary model for the hardest reasoning tasks, and open models for the bulk of the workloads. So the real value proposition is flexibility, not being locked into a single provider. That's very similar to what we saw with open-source data systems like Spark, where openness became a big reason enterprises adopted it.

r002.rationale: It says enterprises can run open models in their own cloud or on-premises, and that regulated data cannot leave certain boundaries, explaining the benefit of bringing the model to the data.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a few things, and they're really the same things that made open source win in infrastructure more broadly, whether that's Linux, or Spark, or Kubernetes.

The first one is control. When you're an enterprise and you're building on top of a proprietary model, you're building on something you don't control. The model can change underneath you, the pricing can change, the terms of service can change. We've seen this already, where a provider updates a model and suddenly the behavior of your application shifts and you have no idea why. With an open model, you pin the weights, you own that artifact. Nobody can take it away from you or deprecate it.

The second is data. For many enterprises, the data is the most valuable asset they have, and they're very reluctant to send it outside their boundaries. With an open model, you can run it in your own environment, on-prem, in your VPC, wherever you want. And more importantly, you can fine-tune it on your own data. And this is where I think the real value is. If you look at what enterprises actually need, it's not a model that's good at everything. It's a model that's really good at their particular task, their particular domain, their particular workflows. And when you specialize a smaller open model on your data, you can get quality that matches or exceeds the frontier proprietary models for that task, at a fraction of the cost and latency.

Which brings me to the third point, which is cost. When you deploy at scale, inference cost dominates. If you have a smaller model that's fine-tuned for your use case, you can run it on much cheaper hardware, you can batch it, you can optimize it however you want. You're not paying a premium for capabilities you don't use.

And then there's the ecosystem argument. Once you have open weights, you get this whole community building tooling around them, quantization, serving systems like vLLM, evaluation frameworks, all of that. The pace of innovation is just faster because many more people can participate. So you're not depending on one company's roadmap.

Now, I want to be clear, I don't think it's open versus closed, one wins and the other loses. The frontier proprietary models are going to be ahead on the hardest, most general problems for some time. But the gap is closing fast, and for most enterprise workloads you don't need the absolute frontier. You need something good enough that you can control, customize, and afford to run. And for that, open models are a very compelling proposition.

r001.rationale: The response calls enterprise data a valuable asset and says it can be used for fine-tuning, but does not identify it as a source of competitive differentiation.

r002.rationale: The response says enterprises can run open models in their own VPC and explains they are reluctant to send their data outside their boundaries, conveying how this protects confidentiality.

astra-6.text:
I think the value proposition is control and flexibility. Enterprises have their own data, their own requirements, and their own constraints. With an open-source model, they can deploy it in their own environment, keep sensitive data there, and customize the model for the task they care about.

And you don’t necessarily need the most powerful general-purpose model for every task. If you have a well-defined application, a smaller model that you fine-tune can give you the quality you need at a lower cost and with lower latency.

There is also the question of independence. You can choose who runs the model, change your infrastructure, and avoid being tied to a single provider. So it’s not simply that the model is available for free. It’s that you have more control over the economics and over how the technology fits into your business.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value proposition is really about control and flexibility. Enterprises have their own data, their own requirements, and their own constraints. With an open-source model, they can run it in their own environment, customize it for a particular task, and decide how their data is used.

They also have more control over cost. If you have a workload at sufficient scale, you can optimize the model and the infrastructure together. You may not need the largest model for every request; a smaller model adapted to your application can be a very attractive option.

And you’re less dependent on a single provider. You can build expertise and infrastructure that let you take advantage of improvements across the ecosystem. That combination—customization, control over data, and control over economics—is very compelling for enterprises.
